sm: The host, an economist at Harvard, opens a conversation with his guest Allison about the recent Nixon-maxing trend, a reappraisal of Richard Nixon. He says Nixon was once seen as the devil because of Watergate, the enemies list and Vietnam, yet his domestic record was surprisingly liberal: an early disability rights law, the creation of OSHA, and pushing quotas on universities and corporations. Allison says she mostly knows Nixon for leaving the gold standard and imposing price controls, though she credits ending Bretton Woods and opening trade with China. Both call the opening to China one of the big moves in world history, and the host notes that only a committed anti-communist could have done it.

The host explains Bretton Woods, the postwar system in which countries pegged their currencies to the dollar, which could be exchanged for gold. By 1970 the United States lacked the gold to cover its dollars, France wanted its gold, and Vietnam War spending was feeding inflation, so Nixon was forced off the gold standard without a plan. He argues the 1970s inflation came mainly from Nixon pressuring Fed chair Arthur Burns to print money, which the Watergate tapes reveal, rather than from the oil shock. Europeans were furious, and Treasury Secretary John Connally told them the dollar was our currency but their problem. The host adds that Nixon was a master of the political business cycle, including a double indexing of Social Security in an election year.

The host notes that Nixon did not install the White House taping system, since Kennedy and Johnson had used it too. Allison says price controls still bother her, citing a candidate who invoked Nixon to argue for national price controls, but she thinks leaving gold brought long-run benefits like low inflation, financial derivatives and cheaper goods. The host says the China shock accounted for only a small share of job turnover. He recalls hating the Vietnam War and fearing his own draft number, and says Nixon wanted out but took a long time. He argues that Nixon was a Keynesian facing war costs and oil shocks, and that top economists like James Tobin and Richard Cooper urged stimulus, which made inflation worse.

The host argues that the system was going to break regardless, since Johnson's Great Society and the war meant deficits, and there was not enough gold. Inflation persisted under Ford and Carter, whom he calls men of integrity but weak presidents. Economists at the time, including Paul Samuelson, misdiagnosed the oil shock as a demand shock when it was a supply shock, a parallel he draws to today. He also praises Nixon for not contesting the 1960 election against Kennedy despite fraud claims, saying the country could not take the strain. He says he studies Nixon as a model of politicians who buy a pre-election sugar high, while also admiring the China opening.

Allison suggests Nixon should be the host's hero as the creator of floating exchange rates, and the host jokes about a Nixon mask. He recalls being a chess player in Poland when Nixon resigned, and Eastern European players found the idea of resigning over tapes absurd. They discuss how Nixon was conservative but eclectic, saying we are all Keynesians now and borrowing the Democratic playbook, much as Trump is no small-government conservative. The host says China's rise reduced global inequality and may have hastened the end of the Cold War, and tells a Kissinger story about Mao turning to America. His lesson is that no law protects against a president's poor character, though Congress rein in presidential power after Nixon.

The host notes that Nixon faced a Democratic House and Senate throughout his presidency yet got a lot done. There were fifty-six Democrats in the Senate, impeachment conviction needs sixty-seven, and enough Republicans told Nixon they would vote to impeach that he retreated. He says party loyalty today leaves little room for deals, which feeds the debt problem. He says people should not be canceled forever, and that history deserves a fuller look. He explains that he supported George McGovern in 1972, who lost forty-nine states, because of the draft and Vietnam. He also says Carter's Fed appointee Bill Miller made Arthur Burns look like Paul Volcker, and that Nixon gets blamed for things that began earlier.

The speakers say economists constantly rethink history, and the host says he never expected to call Nixon's record mixed. He would not predict that tariff wars will look good later, and Allison guesses tariffs might at best open a new way of thinking about commerce. He calls himself an unabashed globalist and says America cannot retreat from the world. They say ideas from the 1970s, such as capital controls and currency manipulation, may return. The host adds that Nixon-era defense spending reached about fifteen percent of GDP, versus about three percent now, and nobody knew Russia would prove a paper tiger. Asked whether Nixon was a risk maxer, Allison says leaving gold was a forced risk, and that he was part of an era of trying to manage risk.

Allison argues that from the mid-sixties government began removing risk from people's lives, with price controls, capital controls and the EPA. The host replies that some of Nixon's programs addressed real externalities, such as OSHA, disability protections, Social Security indexing and aid for the blind. Allison distinguishes insurance, which she says encourages upside risk-taking, from hedging that removes risk altogether, and she places the EPA and OSHA in the second group. The host says students now ask about safe spaces, and Allison describes a generational decline in risk taking from boomers to millennials. They tie the Nixon revival to lower moral standards and cheating, concluding that his record is mixed and credit him for currency, capital flows and globalization.
